title: Given an array of `n+1` integers where each integer is in the range `1` to `n`, exactly one number is repeated (possibly multiple times). Find the duplicate without modifying the array if required, and discuss both the Cyclic Sort and Floyd's cycle approaches.
shortTitle: Find the Duplicate Number (Single Repeated Value in 1..n)
keyPoints: The pigeonhole principle guarantees a duplicate when n+1 values are drawn from the range 1 to n.
Cyclic Sort places each value at index value-1; when the home slot already holds the same value, that is the duplicate.
Cyclic Sort mutates the array and runs in O(n) time with O(1) space.
Floyd's tortoise-and-hare treats values as next-index pointers, finds the cycle entry, which is the duplicate, without modifying the array.
Floyd's is the correct choice when the array must remain read-only.
Binary search on the value range with pigeonhole counting is a third O(n log n) read-only option.

s1_definition.oneliner: Place each value at its home index; the first time the home already holds that same value, you have found the duplicate.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Problem** – an array of n+1 integers in range 1..n has exactly one repeated value; find it.
- **Pigeonhole principle** – more values than slots guarantees at least one repeat.
- **Cyclic Sort** – place value v at index v-1; when the home already holds v, that is the duplicate. Mutates the array.
- **Floyd's cycle** – treat values as next-index pointers, detect the cycle entry. Does not mutate the array.
- **Trade-off** – Cyclic Sort is simpler but destroys input; Floyd's is read-only but harder to justify.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has one more loan application than it has application numbers, so by simple counting at least one number was reused. A clerk files each application in its numbered slot, and the first time they find a slot already holding the same application number, that is the reused number.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Cyclic Sort Approach:
  nums = [3, 1, 3, 4, 2]

  i=0: nums[0]=3, home=2, nums[2]=3
       nums[0] == nums[2] --> DUPLICATE = 3

  Floyd's Cycle Approach:
  nums = [1, 3, 4, 2, 2]
  Index: 0  1  2  3  4
  Value: 1  3  4  2  2

  Pointer chain: 0->1->3->2->4->2->4->2 (cycle at 2)

  Phase 1 (meet inside cycle):
  slow: 1 -> 3 -> 2
  fast: 3 -> 2 -> 2
  Meet at 2

  Phase 2 (find entry):
  finder: 0 -> 1 -> 3 -> 2
  slow:   2 -> 4 -> 2
  Meet at 2 = DUPLICATE

  Decision Tree:
  ┌──────────────────┐
  │ Mutation allowed? │
  └────┬────────┬─────┘
       YES      NO
       │        │
  Cyclic Sort   ├─ O(1) space? --> Floyd's
                └─ O(n) space? --> HashSet
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the single duplicate in an array of n+1 values drawn from the range 1 to n starts with the pigeonhole principle: more values than available numbers guarantees a repeat. If I am allowed to mutate the array, I use Cyclic Sort, placing each value at the index equal to the value minus one. The instant I try to send a value home and find the same value already sitting there, that value is the duplicate.

When the array must stay intact, I switch to Floyd's tortoise-and-hare. I treat each value as a pointer from index i to index nums[i], which turns the array into a functional graph with a guaranteed cycle. Floyd's two-phase algorithm finds the cycle entry, which is the duplicate, in O(n) time and O(1) space without writing to the array.

I always present both approaches in an interview and state the deciding factor: Cyclic Sort when mutation is acceptable and clarity matters, Floyd's when the array is read-only. Binary search on the value range is a third option at O(n log n) for when Floyd's is too complex under time pressure.

In my work at the National Bank of India, this guarded the loan application feed where a glitch occasionally reused one application number. Downstream approval steps re-read the original array, so mutation was not acceptable, and Floyd's cycle detection found the duplicate without touching the input.

Remember one sentence: Cyclic Sort finds the duplicate by placing values at home indices (mutates), Floyd's finds it by detecting the cycle in the value-as-pointer graph (read-only), and the pigeonhole principle guarantees a repeat exists.
